Tenth Indian Expedition to Antarctica, Scientific Report, 1995 
Department of Ocean Development, Technical Publication No. 8, pp. 159-180 
Report on the Participation by the Bhabha Atomic Research
Centre in the Tenth Indian Expedition to Antarctica
T. V. RAMACHANDRAN AND M.C. BALANI
Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, Bombay
Abstract
The Antarctic continent can be expected to provide reference levels for all environmental and
pollution studies due to its remoteness and restricted human activities. The Bhabha Atomic Research
Centre has participated in the Xth Expedition primarily to collect background baseline data on natural
radioactivity, heavy metal concentration in soil and water, and biological specimens. While radioac-
tivity data and some limited heavy metal concentration data have already been collected on air, water
and soil samples from participation in 8th and 9th expeditions: this is the first time BARC made
attempts to collect biological samples as well. Fairly complete data base has been built up on all these
samples and these are presented in this report. The analytical procedures followed at BARC were
mainly by the use of standard chemicals and approved standardisation techniques in case of inorganic
parameters and standard reference gases, wherever required.
Introduction
Man's impact on the oceanic environment has always been the cause for great
concern. Several investigations on the natural radioactivity levels and on the heavy
metal concentrations over the ocean as well as on remote locations have been
carried out by various nations in the world. In order to obtain a background baseline
data over the South Indian ocean and on the Antarctic continent, extensive sampling
has been carried out on air, water, soil, and other environmental samples from
BARC participation in the Xth Expedition during November 27,1990 to March 26,
1991.
Natural Radioactivity Levels in the Atmosphere
Radon (Rn222) and its short lived daughters are the most important radionuclides
present in the ambient as well as in indoor atmosphere from the point of view of
radiation risk to the population. Extensive measurements of natural radioactivity222 220 
levels in the atmosphere due to Rn and Thoron (Rn ) have been carried out
222
enroute to and at Antarctic to obtain the Rn levels pr evailing over Arabian sea
and South Indian ocean region as well as around the Antarctic continent. The
160 T,V. Ramachandran and M.C. Balani 
measurement consists of collection of air particulate matter on a glass fiber filter of
size 5 inch diameter (having a collection efficiency of 100 % for short-lived Rn
daughters), for a known period of time (two hours duration) using a high volume
sampler of 450 liters per minute, installed at the front foxil of the research vessel.
This location is selected to avoid external contamination from the ship boilers and
kitchen. The collected filter paper sample is counted for its gross alpha activity
using a ZnS(Ag) counter of 35% counting efficiency, of 0.45 cpm as background.
From the gross alpha counts, the Rn222 levels were estimated taking into account
the collection time, flow rate, counting efficiency, the period of collection and also
assuming radioactive equilibrium among the short lived daughters, which is valid
over the ocean surfaces.
On an average, six to seven air particulate samples at periodic interval of time
per day were collected and analysed. The overall errors due to  sampling and
processing is about ±25 %. The sampling was also carried out at Antarctica. In all
338 air particulate samples were collected during the cruise. Estimated ambient
Rn222 levels are summarised in Table 1. Measured Rn222 levels were found to
decrease steadily from 2.4 Bq m-3 at Goa, to 0.04 Bq m-3 at the equator and to 0.0159
Bq m-3 towards 70°S. Around Indian Antarctic station, Maitri, it varied from 0.02
to 0.030 Bq m-3 with a mean of 0.0296 Bq m-3.
Extremely low concentration, observed consistently of the order of 0.037 Bq m-3
from 20° S downwards to South pole, is mainly due to the long path length and time
taken for the air masses to travel to reach the South pole. This can also be due to the
shift of south east trades below the equator and to the westerly wind towards 40° S.
Extremely low concentrations of observed atmospheric radioactivity, due to Rn222
and its short-lived daughters, have to be taken into account while evaluating the
budget of Rn222 in the atmosphere as well as the possible levels of pure maritime
air. These are also very useful in evaluating the residence times and the continental
components in maritime air due to mixing. Decreasing trend of Rn222 levels towards
South pole shows the prevalence of maritime air with long trajectories over the
